summary: Describes a preemption priority policy element for signaled admission protocols such as RSVP and COPS.

plainLanguage.summary: When a router is asked to carry more traffic than it has room for, it has to choose. This document defines the piece of information that says how important each request is: a priority number that a new flow is compared on, and another number that an admitted flow defends itself with. It also defines how the numbers are combined when two requests are joined into one, so that one flow does not pick up a priority it never paid for.

questions: what is the difference between preemption and defending priority
subtitle: How a preemption priority travels in an RSVP or COPS message, and what happens when two flows are merged.

tldr.problem: When more flows ask for admission than a node can carry, something has to give. Capacity-based admission control simply admits the first arrivals, and policy-based admission control needs a way to say which of the competing flows matter most.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines a policy element, PREEMPTION_PRI, with a 16-bit preemption priority and a 16-bit defending priority, a merging strategy and an error code. A policy decision point creates the element, local decision points merge them, and policy enforcement points use them to admit or preempt flows.
tldr.outcome: The element is stateless, so it can be carried in COPS without any history, and the merging rules keep a merged flow from gaining or losing priority unfairly. The P-Type value 1 is registered with IANA.

today: RFC 3181 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2001. It replaced RFC 2751, which defined the same element, and it registers the P-Type value 1 with IANA. The element itself travels inside the policy data objects defined in RFC 2750, and the decision and enforcement roles are set out in RFC 2753.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This document describes a preemption priority policy element for use by signaled policy-based admission protocols such as RSVP and COPS.

Traditional capacity-based admission control indiscriminately admits new flows until capacity is exhausted, admitting the first that arrive. Policy-based admission control tries to reduce the significance of the order of arrival and uses policy-based admission criteria instead. One of the more popular policy criteria is the rank of importance of a flow relative to the others competing for admission into a network node.

Preemption priority takes effect only when the flows attempting admission through a node overbook the resources, so that capacity-based admission control would have to reject some of them. The priority criterion then helps the node select the most important flows, those with the highest priority, for admission, while rejecting the low priority ones. Network nodes that support preemption should consider preempting previously admitted low-priority flows to make room for a newer, high-priority flow.
sections.plainLanguage: Admission control is the decision about which new traffic a node accepts when it is already full. The usual rule is first come, first served, which says nothing about which traffic matters more. This document adds a number to each request that says how important it is, so the node can keep the important traffic and drop the rest.

sections.title: Scope and Applicability
sections.content:
The framework document for policy-based admission control describes the components that take part in policy decision making: the PDP, the PEP and the LDP. The emphasis on PREEMPTION_PRI elements is that they be simple, stateless and light-weight, so that they could be implemented inside a node's local decision point.

Three assumptions shape how the elements are used. They are created by policy decision points. In a model where the PDP controls the PEPs at the edge of the policy domain, such as in border routers, the PDP reduces the relevant sets of policy rules to a single priority criterion, and that priority, expressed in the PREEMPTION_PRI element, is then communicated to the downstream PEPs of the same policy domain, which have local decision points but no controlling PDP.

They can be processed by local decision points. An LDP may interpret the objects, forward them as they are, or perform local merging to forward an equivalent merged element. LDPs must follow the merging strategy that the PDP encoded in the objects. A PDP, being a superset of an LDP, may act as an LDP as well.

They are enforced by policy enforcement points. The elements interact with the node's traffic control module, and with capacity admission control, to enforce the priorities and to preempt previously admitted flows when the need arises.
sections.plainLanguage: Three kinds of component are involved. A policy decision point works out how important a flow is and puts the number into the message. A local decision point in the middle of the network merges the numbers of the flows it combines, following the rule the decision point chose. A policy enforcement point is the router that admits or rejects the traffic and, when needed, preempts a lower priority flow that is already running.

sections.title: Stateless Policy
sections.content: Signaled preemption priority is stateless: it does not require past history or external information to be interpreted. When it is carried in COPS messages for the outsourcing of policy decisions, the objects are therefore included as COPS Stateless Policy Data Decision objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The priority number travels with the request and stands on its own. Nothing has to be remembered about earlier flows for it to be understood, which is what lets it be carried in a COPS message without any extra bookkeeping.

sections.title: Policy Element Format
sections.content:
The format of Policy Data objects is defined in the RSVP extensions document, and a single Policy Data object may contain one or more policy elements, each representing a different and perhaps orthogonal policy. The preemption priority policy element is 12 octets long and carries a length, a policy type, some flags, a merging strategy, an error code, and the two priorities.

The length is 16 bits and is always 12, the length of the element in bytes. The P-Type is 16 bits and is 1 for PREEMPTION_PRI, a value registered with IANA. The flags field is 8 bits and is reserved, always zero. The merge strategy is 8 bits: 1 for taking the priority of the highest quality of service, which is recommended; 2 for taking the highest priority, which is described as aggressive; and 3 for forcing an error on a heterogeneous merge. The error code is 8 bits: 0 for NO_ERROR, the value used in a regular element; 1 for PREEMPTION, meaning a previously admitted flow was preempted; and 2 for HETEROGENEOUS, meaning the element met a heterogeneous merge. A final reserved octet is always zero.

The preemption priority is 16 bits and unsigned. It is the priority of the new flow compared with the defending priority of previously admitted flows, and higher values mean higher priority. The defending priority is also 16 bits and unsigned. Once a flow has been admitted, its preemption priority is irrelevant, and its defending priority is used to compare with the preemption priority of new flows. For any specific flow, the preemption priority must always be less than or equal to the defending priority. A wide gap between the two provides extra stability: a moderate preemption priority makes it harder for a flow to preempt others, but once it has succeeded, the higher defending priority makes it easier for the flow to avoid being preempted itself. That is the mechanism for balancing order dependency against priority.
sections.plainLanguage: The element is 12 bytes. It carries two 16-bit numbers. The first is used when a flow asks to be admitted, and the second once it has been admitted: the second is the priority the flow defends itself with. The flow may ask for less priority than it defends, and the gap between the two is what stops a flow from being knocked out as soon as it has knocked something else out.

sections.title: Priority Merging Issues
sections.content:
Consider two RSVP reservations that merge. F1 has a high quality of service and a low priority, and F2 has a low quality of service and a high priority. The merged reservation F3 should have the high quality of service, but what priority should it take? The document identifies three kinds of unwanted effect.

The free-rider problem arises if F3 takes the high priority: F1 then got a free ride, assuming a high priority that was only intended for the low quality of service F2. If cost is a function of quality of service and priority, F1 receives an expensive priority without having to pay for it. Denial of service is the inverse, and arises if F3 takes the low priority: the merged flow could be preempted or fail even though F2 presented a high priority. One free-rider turns out to be another's denial of service. Instability comes from the combination of preemption priority, the killer reservation and the blockade state, which may increase the instability of admitted flows, where a reservation is preempted, reinstated and preempted again periodically.

In a merging situation a local decision point may receive several preemption elements and must compute the priority of the merged flow. Preemption priority and defending priority are merged and computed separately, irrespective of each other. All the priority elements are examined according to their merging strategy to decide whether they should take part, and the highest priority of all the participating elements is the result.

Three strategies are defined. Take priority of highest QoS: the element takes part only if its flow contributed to the merged quality of service, that is, if its quality of service requirement is not a subset of another reservation. A simple way to tell is to compute the merged quality of service with and without it and compare. The reasoning is that the highest quality of service flow dominates the merged reservation, so its priority should dominate it too, and this approach is the most amenable to preventing priority distortions such as free-riders and denial of service. It is a recommended strategy.

Take highest priority: every element takes part. This disassociates priority from the quality of service level and is therefore highly subject to free-riders and to denial of service, the inverse image. It is not a recommended method, but it may be simpler to implement. Force error on heterogeneous merge: an element may take part only if all the other flows in the merged reservation have the same quality of service level. The reasoning is that the heterogeneous case is relatively rare and too complicated to deal with, so it is better prohibited, though this strategy lends itself to denial of service, when a single receiver specifying a non-compatible quality of service level may cause denial of service for all the other receivers. It is a recommended strategy when reservation homogeneity is coordinated and enforced for the whole multicast tree, and it is more restrictive than the first strategy but easier to implement. The determination of heterogeneous flows applies to the quality of service level only, that is, the FLOWSPEC values, and is a matter for local definition.

The document also says how elements may be modified on the way. When Policy Data objects are protected by integrity, LDPs should not modify them, and must forward them as they are or the security envelope would be invalidated. In other cases LDPs may modify and merge the incoming elements to reduce their size and number. Merging is performed for each merging strategy separately, because there is no known algorithm to merge elements of different strategies without losing information that may affect other nodes. For each strategy, the highest quality of service of all the participating elements is taken and placed in an outgoing element of that strategy, which compresses the number of forwarded elements to at most the number of different merging strategies, whatever the number of receivers.
sections.plainLanguage: When two requests are joined, the combined request has to end up with one priority, and either choice can be unfair. The document offers three rules. The recommended one keeps only the priorities of the requests that actually set the combined service level, so a high service level does not drag a high priority along with it. The simplest rule takes the highest priority of all the requests, and is open to both kinds of unfairness. The third refuses to merge requests whose service levels differ.

sections.title: Error Processing
sections.content:
A PREEMPTION_PRI error object is sent back toward the appropriate receivers when an error involving PREEMPTION_PRI elements occurs.

With the PREEMPTION error, a previously admitted flow has been preempted. A copy of the preempting flow's PREEMPTION_PRI element is sent back toward the PDP that originated the preempted object. That PDP has information on both the preempting and the preempted priorities, and may construct a higher priority element in an effort to re-instate the preempted flow.

With the Heterogeneity error, a flow that has the heterogeneous error merging strategy set in its element meets heterogeneity, and the element is sent back toward the receivers with the heterogeneity error code set.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things are reported back. When a running flow is knocked out, the decision point that asked for it is told, with the details of the flow that took its place, so that it can ask for a better priority and get the flow back. When a merge turns out to be of the kind a flow said it could not handle, that flow's element is sent back with the error code set.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The integrity of PREEMPTION_PRI is guaranteed, as for any other policy element, by its encapsulation into a Policy Data object.

Further security mechanisms are not warranted, especially since preemption priority aims to give simple and quick guidance to routers within a trusted zone, or at least a single zone, and no zone boundaries are crossed.
sections.plainLanguage: The element inherits whatever protection the surrounding policy data object has, and the document asks for nothing more: the priority is meant to guide routers inside one trusted area, where an attacker has no business being.

viz.caption: THE PREEMPTION PRIORITY POLICY ELEMENT, 12 BYTES

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Always 12, the length of the element in bytes.

fields.name: M. Strategy
fields.desc: 1 takes the priority of the highest QoS, 2 takes the highest priority, 3 forces an error on a heterogeneous merge.

fields.name: Error Code
fields.desc: 0 no error, 1 a flow was preempted, 2 a heterogeneous merge was met.

fields.name: Preemption Priority
fields.desc: The priority of the new flow, compared with the defending priority of admitted flows. Higher is more important.

fields.name: Defending Priority
fields.desc: The priority an admitted flow defends itself with. Never lower than the preemption priority of the same flow.

viz.caption: THE TWO PRIORITIES AND WHAT THEY ARE USED FOR

left.title: Preemption priority
left.desc: Used when a flow asks for admission, and compared with the defending priority of the flows already admitted.

right.title: Defending priority
right.desc: Used once a flow is admitted, and compared with the preemption priority of the flows that arrive later.

viz.caption: THE MERGING STRATEGIES AND ERROR CODES

items.label: Merge strategy
items.desc: Take priority of highest QoS. Recommended.

items.label: Error code
items.desc: NO_ERROR, the value used for a regular element.

items.label: Error code
items.desc: PREEMPTION: a previously admitted flow was preempted.

items.label: Error code
items.desc: HETEROGENEOUS: the element met a heterogeneous merge.

items.title: Take priority of highest QoS
items.text: Only the elements of the flows that set the merged service level take part. Recommended.

items.title: Take highest priority
items.text: Every element takes part, whatever the service level. Simpler, but open to free-riders.

items.title: Force error on heterogeneous merge
items.text: Only elements whose flows all have the same service level take part; otherwise an error is reported.

viz.caption: WHAT GOES WRONG IN A MERGE

items.title: Free-rider
items.text: The merged flow takes the high priority of one leg, so that leg gets a priority it never paid for.

items.title: Denial of service
items.text: The merged flow takes the low priority, so a flow that presented high priority can still be dropped.

items.title: Instability
items.text: A reservation is preempted, reinstated and preempted again, over and over.
